title: Street Glide vs Road Glide
excerpt: Batwing vs sharknose — how fork-mounted and frame-mounted fairings change the bagger experience.

sections.heading: The short version
sections.body: Both are Harley Touring baggers with saddlebags and similar powertrains across generations. The big difference is the fairing: Road Glide mounts the fairing to the frame (sharknose); Street Glide mounts it to the forks (batwing). That changes how the bike feels in crosswinds and how the handlebars respond.

sections.heading: Road Glide — frame-mounted fairing
sections.body: Riders often describe Road Glides as calmer at highway speed and more planted in wind. The frame-mounted fairing keeps mass off the forks. Great if you do long interstate miles or ride in open Midwestern weather.

sections.heading: Street Glide — fork-mounted fairing
sections.body: Street Glides tend to feel more traditional and connected through the bars. Many riders prefer the batwing look. If you want the classic bagger silhouette and a slightly more lively front end, this is usually the starting point.

sections.heading: How to decide
sections.body: Sit on both. Take a short test ride if you can. Ask about year, mileage, service history, and mods — those matter more than the badge on the fairing. When you're ready, talk to Joe about what's actually available.

faqs.question: Is one better for Wisconsin highway wind?
faqs.answer: Many riders prefer Road Glide manners in open wind, but preference is personal. Sit on both and ride if you can — Joe can help you compare real units on the floor.

faqs.question: Do they cost the same used?
faqs.answer: Price depends on year, mileage, options, and condition — not the fairing alone. Look at live inventory and ask Joe for a clear number on the bike you want.

title: Softail vs Sportster
excerpt: Chassis intent, size, and who each family usually fits — without inventing which one 'sells better.'

sections.heading: Different jobs
sections.body: Sportsters are typically lighter and simpler entry points. Softails use a different chassis feel with more cruiser/Touring-adjacent comfort depending on the model. Start with how far you ride and whether you need passenger room.

sections.heading: Fit and confidence
sections.body: Seat height, reach, and weight matter more than badges. A short or new rider may prefer a manageable Sportster; a taller rider or two-up tourist may lean Softail or Touring. Try before you buy.

sections.heading: Used buying notes
sections.body: Confirm year, motor family, service records, and mods. Modern Sportster S / Nightster platforms differ from classic air-cooled Sportsters — compare apples to apples.

faqs.question: Which is better for a first Harley?
faqs.answer: Many first-timers start on Sportsters, but the right bike is the one you can ride confidently. Talk through distance, passenger needs, and budget with Joe.

faqs.question: Can I grow out of a Sportster?
faqs.answer: Some riders keep a Sportster forever; others move to Softail or Touring later. Buy for how you'll ride for the next few years, not a hypothetical forever bike.
